# The Unexpected Profundity of Doing Dishes

I've been thinking about dishes lately, which might sound like the most boring direction a mind could wander, but bear with me. There's something about the mundane that deserves more of our attention than we typically give it.

It started on a Tuesday evening when my dishwasher broke. Nothing catastrophic—just a mechanical failure that would cost more to repair than replace. Standing in my kitchen surrounded by the usual casualties of daily living (coffee mugs, dinner plates, the mysterious bowls we all accumulate), I faced a choice: buy a new one or wash dishes by hand while I sorted things out. Something made me choose the second option.

The first night, I was impatient. I wanted to optimize, to find the most efficient method possible. My mind was elsewhere—on work emails, on plans, on the thousand small anxieties that usually inhabit the background of my consciousness. But by the third night, something shifted. I wasn't thinking about efficiency anymore. I was just... washing dishes.

There's a peculiar meditation in it, I discovered. Your hands follow a simple pattern: soap, scrub, rinse, repeat. The warm water becomes almost comfortable, almost comforting. The foam dissipates. The plates transform from dirty to clean, and unlike so much of modern life, the before-and-after is immediate and undeniable. You can see what you've accomplished. You can hold it in your hands.

I started to understand why my grandmother, who passed away years ago, seemed to enjoy this task. She had a dishwasher—several, actually, as different models came through her kitchen over the decades—but she often insisted on hand-washing the "good dishes." I thought it was stubbornness or nostalgia, but maybe it was something else. Maybe it was intentionality. Maybe it was the desire to do something with her hands that she could directly control and observe.

In our contemporary world, we're obsessed with outsourcing, with automating, with making everything faster. We treat the time saved as pure gain, pure freedom. And sometimes it is. But I think we've collectively underestimated what we lose when we remove the friction from everything. The friction is where the thinking happens. The friction is where you process things.

I've noticed this in other areas too. People used to walk places and think. They'd use the time to organize their thoughts, to let their mind wander productively. Now, if walking takes longer than driving, we view it as a loss. We plug in earbuds or podcasts to make the time "productive," filling every silence with input. I'm not against podcasts—I listen to them too—but there's something happening when we can't sit with ourselves for five minutes without stimulation.

The dishes gave me that. Not because I'm some Zen master (I'm absolutely not), but because they were boring enough that my brain stopped fighting for entertainment and started just... existing.

It made me think about the difference between loneliness and solitude, which I think is one of the most important distinctions we fail to make. Loneliness is a state of unwanted isolation. Solitude is chosen aloneness. Solitude is valuable. It's where reflection happens, where creativity genuinely originates, where you remember what your own thoughts actually sound like without the constant chorus of external input.

But here's the thing I've realized: I don't think you need to go on a silent retreat to find solitude. You don't need to move to a cabin in the woods. You just need dishes. Or folding laundry. Or gardening. Or walking without a podcast. You need something that occupies just enough of your surface-level attention that your deeper mind is free to roam.

Of course, I also recognize the privilege in this realization. There's a certain luxury in finding washing dishes meditative rather than exhausting. If you're working multiple jobs, managing childcare, dealing with genuine hardship, the last thing you want to hear is that your daily tasks are actually opportunities for enlightenment. That's tone-deaf at best, infuriating at worst. I'm not suggesting that struggle is secretly wonderful or that difficulty is just opportunity in disguise. Some things are just hard, and there's no meditation required to endure them—just survival.

But for those of us living in relative comfort, I think we've made a bargain that maybe isn't serving us. We've traded friction for convenience and lost something in the transaction. We've outsourced so many small tasks that we've outsourced our solitude too.

My new dishwasher is being delivered next week, and I'll probably install it. I'm not so committed to hand-washing that I want to spend hours on it daily. But I think I'll keep doing it sometimes anyway. Intentionally. Like people used to knit or whittle, not because they needed to (they could buy clothes and wood carvings), but because the activity itself was valuable.

This is what I think we're missing: the understanding that not every moment needs to be optimized. Not every activity needs to be in service to a larger goal. Sometimes the point is just to do the thing. To feel the warm water, to watch the dirt disappear, to end up with something clean. To be present in your own life rather than constantly accelerating through it toward some future moment where you're finally comfortable enough to relax.

The irony, of course, is that the future moment never comes. There's always something else. Always another thing to optimize, to achieve, to worry about.

So I'll keep washing dishes. Not for enlightenment, not as some grand philosophical statement, but simply because it turns out I actually enjoy it. And maybe that's the most profound thing of all: discovering that the things we thought we had to escape are actually worth our time, after all.
